amendments.rule: Where a clause carries a redundant Greek negative — `οὐ` with a following negative word, whether a negative indefinite such as `οὐδέν` or `οὐδὲ ἕν` or a negative adverb such as `οὐκέτι` — and the ASV realizes the negation once, in that following word, that word takes the whole English negation and `οὐ` is its own `unrepresented` unit. `οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν … οὐδέν` → *The Son can do nothing* gives *nothing* to `οὐδέν` and nothing to `οὐ`, as `Οὐ δύναμαι ἐγὼ ποιεῖν … οὐδέν` → *I can of myself do nothing* and `Οὐ δύναται ἄνθρωπος λαμβάνειν οὐδὲ ἕν` → *A man can receive nothing* do, and as `καὶ οὐκ εἶδεν αὐτὸν οὐκέτι ὁ εὐνοῦχος` → *and the eunuch saw him no more* gives *no more* to `οὐκέτι` and nothing to `οὐκ`. Rule 59 carries this to `μή` and states the licensing test, which is the whole of this rule: the following word must itself be a negative able to carry the English negation alone, which is why an adverb serves as well as an indefinite and why a plain `τις` or `τι` does not. Do not split the English negation across the two, and do not join them into one unit: the two negatives are not adjacent, and what stands between them is the verb and its complements. Where the ASV writes an English word for content of the negator's own that the negation does not absorb, the negator is not emptied but keeps that word as its own `aligned` unit: `οὐδέπω γὰρ ἦν ἐπ᾽ οὐδενὶ αὐτῶν ἐπιπεπτωκός` → *for as yet it was fallen upon none of them* gives *as yet* to `οὐδέπω` and *none* to `οὐδενί`, the temporal element being no part of what *none* carries. Rule 33's `οὐ μή` is the contrast and it is a narrow one — there the particles stand side by side and the English negation answers to the pair, so they are one `noncompositional` unit. Where the ASV instead spells the negation into the modal, `οὐ δύναται` → *cannot* stays one `aligned` unit under rule 39 and the question does not arise. Rule 69 is untouched: where the ASV renders the following negative non-negatively, as *any* or *any man*, it cannot carry the negation alone and the negator keeps the English word that does. A reference comparison will report the `unrepresented` `οὐ` as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.
amendments.why: Rule 41 names only a negative indefinite, and ACT.8.39 met a negative adverb: `οὐκ … οὐκέτι` → *no more* leaves `οὐκ` empty on exactly the reasoning rule 41 gives for `οὐδέν`. Rule 59 already states the licensing test in general terms — that the second word is itself a negative able to carry the English negation alone — so this widens rule 41 where it stands instead of leaving a verse pass to infer the adverb case from a rule scoped to `μή`. The second addition comes from ACT.8.16, where `οὐδέπω` is not emptied because the ASV writes *as yet* for its temporal element while `οὐδενί` → *none* carries the negation; that is the same principle stated from the other side and stops a later pass emptying a negator that still has English of its own. Nothing in the corpus extract contradicts either arm, and no existing reading changes: rules 33, 39 and 69 are quoted back unaltered.

conventions: εὐαγγελίζομαι: where the ASV renders the lexeme by a single English word, that word takes the whole unit and the head (8:4 preaching, 8:35 preached); where it writes a light verb plus a noun, the head is the noun that glosses the lexeme under rule 91 — tidings at 8:12 (preaching good tidings), gospel at 8:25 and 8:40 (preached the gospel). Heading such a unit on preaching or preached is the competing reading and was not taken.

Periphrastic finite verb plus participle splits into two units: the finite verb keeps the English auxiliary and any supplied subject pronoun, the participle keeps the lexical verb — 8:1 ἦν → was / συνευδοκῶν → consenting, 8:16 ἦν → it was / ἐπιπεπτωκός → fallen and ὑπῆρχον → they had been / βεβαπτισμένοι → baptized, 8:28 ἦν → he was / ὑποστρέφων and καθήμενος. Where the ASV collapses the periphrasis into a simple tense and writes no auxiliary at all, the finite verb keeps only the supplied subject: 8:13 ἦν → he, προσκαρτερῶν → continued. Joining the pair into one unit headed on the lexical verb is the competing reading and was not taken.

A supplied juncture and converting a Greek participle into a coordinate member rides with the member it introduces and is never added, in this chapter for coordinate finite clauses (8:5, 8:24, 8:27, 8:30, 8:34) and equally at 8:31, where the ASV coordinates the participle ἀναβάντα with the infinitive καθίσαι and the and goes to καθίσαι. Rule 98's added reading was weighed and refused there, its scope being an asyndetic seam between two like constituents both rendered alike.

report: Read all 70 candidate groups end to end. No genuine cross-verse split: every multi-treatment bucket is licensed either by the ASV rendering one word differently or by a different Greek construction. The groups I checked hardest were εὐαγγελίζω (8:4, 8:12, 8:25, 8:35, 8:40 — a single English word takes the head, a phrase heads on the noun glossing the lexeme, one policy throughout), rule 31's preposed vs postposed article (8:14 vs 8:1), rule 106's preverb particle vs an expressed preposition (8:3, 8:24, 8:39), the substantival article before a participle (8:6 and 8:7 split identically), rule 85's complementizer (8:9, 8:23), and the two arms of rule 20, which 8:33 writes out in one verse.

The table is blind to `added` units, so I read the dump for the fold/add split it cannot show. The chapter has no `added` unit anywhere, and each supplied English word carries a licensing token: *from* on Πολλῶν (8:7), *under* on Κανδάκης (8:27), *here is* on ὕδωρ (8:36), *him* on προσδραμών (8:30), the repeated *in* on σύνδεσμον (8:23, rule 103). No verse folds what another verse would have marked added.

One correction, in 8:31. The supplied *and* before *sit* sits on καθίσαι — the same placement as the five rule 88 junctures at 8:5, 8:24, 8:27, 8:30 and 8:34 — but the note cites rule 29, which rule 98 names by number and refuses as a general licence. The edges are unchanged; the note now argues from rule 88 (a subordinate participle stands in the clause and is what the ASV converted into a coordinate member) and names the competing `added` reading under rule 98, as rule 16 requires and the old note did not.

BSB: 10 disagreements, none an error. Nine are articles left unrepresented under rules 20 (8:1, 8:18, 8:22, 8:32), 23 (8:3, 8:6), 31 (8:26), 38 (8:21) and 61 (8:11) — the documented convention difference. The tenth is οὐκ at 8:39, which rule 41 itself says a comparison will report without that being a correction. No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.

Three conventions recorded: the εὐαγγελ- head policy, the periphrastic finite-verb-plus-participle split (8:1, 8:13, 8:16 twice, 8:28), and the chapter's juncture policy including the non-finite case at 8:31. The other thirteen repeated notes the validator flagged are straight citations of rules 20, 21, 23, 32, 38, 51, 61, 70, 86 and 88, which bind every verse already and need no log entry.

One amendment, to rule 41. It names only a negative indefinite; 8:39 met a negative adverb (οὐκ … οὐκέτι → *no more*), and 8:16 met a negator with non-negative content of its own (οὐδέπω → *as yet*, the negation carried by οὐδενί → *none*). Rule 59 already states the licensing test in general terms, so this widens rule 41 where it stands rather than adding a cross-reference.
